analysis.one_liner: Caps retail gasoline at $2.50 a gallon and lets the President ration fuel during shortages.
analysis.headline: The bill died without any vote: referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on September 8, 2005, sent to a subcommittee on September 19, and never heard from again.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced weeks after Hurricane Katrina knocked out Gulf refineries and sent gas prices soaring, the bill would have ordered the President, within 10 days, to impose a temporary rationing system for crude oil and refined fuels and to cap retail gasoline at $2.50 per gallon. It also required allocation plans to keep homes heated and cooled, keep public services and utilities running, protect farms, and let the Secretary of Energy re-trigger the authority if a future fuel emergency is declared. The authority would last at most one year. The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee's subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers — drivers, households paying heating and cooling bills, farms, transit systems, and utilities — would get protection from post-Katrina price spikes, a guaranteed $2.50 per gallon retail price ceiling, and priority fuel delivery during shortages.

how_it_helps.text: Within 10 days of enactment, the President would have to issue a regulation mandating temporary allocation of crude oil and capping retail gasoline sales at $2.50 per gallon.
The allocation rules must prioritize residential heating and cooling, national defense and homeland security, public services including utilities and mass transit, and agricultural operations.
The rules must also prevent undue economic harm to retail and wholesale businesses that depend on fuel supplies.
The Energy Department would develop criteria for declaring future fuel emergencies, and declaring one would automatically revive the allocation authority.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers and refiners, who would have to sell crude and refined products at government-directed prices and quantities rather than market prices; consumers could also face inconvenience if the cap causes shortages or lines at the pump.

drawbacks.text: A $2.50 per gallon price cap set below the post-Katrina market price could create shortages, rationing by waiting in line, or supply gaps — the same problems price controls produced during the 1970s oil crises.
The bill itself requires preserving a competitive petroleum industry and minimizing interference with markets, an acknowledgment that mandatory allocation and price caps carry real economic risks.

The President would gain broad, fast-acting power to direct fuel supplies, revivable in future emergencies, which concentrates significant economic authority in the executive branch for up to a year at a time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing a genuine supply shock, the trade-off is a lower, predictable price and protected deliveries for homes, farms, and public services, at the risk of shortages and lines if the cap sits below the market price. The one-year limit and the requirement to protect the petroleum industry's viability moderate the design risks, but the bill is a blunt instrument — a price ceiling plus rationing is a crude tool compared to targeted relief — and it never got a hearing or a vote, so it was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Louise Slaughter of New York introduced the bill on September 8, 2005, days after Hurricane Katrina damaged Gulf refineries and drove gasoline prices sharply upward.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On September 19, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
No further action was taken; the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with the bill still in subcommittee.
The bill had only two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers and refiners were better off: no rationing mandate or $2.50 price cap was ever imposed, and refined-product sellers continued to charge the higher post-Katrina market prices the bill would have capped.

for.name: Rep. Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 8, 2005, authorizing fuel allocation and a $2.50 gasoline price cap in response to post-Katrina shortages.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 8, 2005, and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 19, 2005, and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill's support was thin — the sponsor plus two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Independent — so no partisan lineup can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required mandatory allocation of their crude and refined products and capped retail gasoline at $2.50 per gallon, limiting prices they could charge during a shortage. Their revenue during the post-Katrina price spike depended on the bill dying.

The cap would limit what stations could charge, but the bill explicitly directs the allocation plan to prevent undue economic harm to the retail and wholesale industry and to keep fuel flowing to them.

The bill requires the allocation plan to maintain public services, including municipally, cooperatively, and investor-owned utilities and mass transportation, giving them fuel priority during shortages.
The bill requires the allocation plan to maintain agricultural operations, protecting farms' fuel supply during an emergency.
